source: Pane, McCaffrey, Slaughter, Steele & Ikemoto (2014) Effectiveness of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I at Scale (abstract via ERIC EJ1024233)
finding: Randomised trial of school pairs in 7 states: no effect in the first year of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I, positive effect in the second year. Significant for high schools, not for middle schools. About 8 percentile points for the median student.
numbers: Year 1: no effect. Year 2: about +8 percentile points. Significant in high schools only. Exact N and per-level effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract text only; full paper blocked (403). Per-level SDs still unverified. Mastery-learning curriculum, not the student model alone.
agent_relevance: A mastery-driven system needs time to pay off. Test any tracker-based routing over more than a few runs, not on the first pass.

source: Pane et al. (2014) Addendum to Effectiveness of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I at Scale, RAND WR-1050 (abstract via ERIC ED559621)
finding: Alternative analyses of the same data gave substantively the same result. High school students in year 2 gained 0.21 SD, significant.
numbers: +0.21 SD (high school, year 2). Alternative analyses 'substantively the same'.
limits: Same data re-analysed by the same group, so it is robustness, not independent replication. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: K14's recalled 'about 0.20 SD in year 2' is now backed by 0.21 SD for high school only; middle school was not significant.

source: VanLehn (2011) The relative effectiveness of human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring systems (abstract via ERIC EJ946764)
finding: Review of experiments. The folk belief was d = 0.3 (answer-based), 1.0 (ITS) and 2.0 (human tutors) against no tutoring. The review did not confirm it: human tutoring d = 0.79, intelligent tutoring systems d = 0.76.
numbers: Human 0.79; ITS 0.76; believed values 0.3 / 1.0 / 2.0. The answer-based value (recalled as 0.31) is NOT in the abstract.
quote: Instead, it found that the effect size of human tutoring was much lower: d = 0.79.
limits: Abstract only. Step-based vs answer-based split and substep values need the body text. Mix of subjects and test alignment.
agent_relevance: Step-level feedback is about as good as a human tutor. Supports checking each step of a chain, not only the final answer.

source: Kulik & Fletcher (2016) Effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems: a meta-analytic review (abstract via ERIC EJ1090502)
finding: Across 50 controlled evaluations the median effect was +0.66 SD (50th to 75th percentile). The gain depended heavily on whether the test was locally developed or standardised. Evaluations with nonconventional controls (6) or flawed implementation (4) showed small effects.
numbers: Median +0.66 SD over 50 evaluations; small effects in the 6 + 4 excluded evaluations.
limits: Abstract only. Local-test inflation: alignment of test and teaching drives results.
agent_relevance: Measure the agent on tests that match what the tracker trained on AND on held-out tests; the gap is the alignment inflation.

source: Ma, Adesope, Nesbit & Liu (2014) Intelligent tutoring systems and learning outcomes: a meta-analysis (abstract via ERIC EJ1049508)
finding: 107 effect sizes, 14,321 participants. ITS beat large-group teaching (g 0.42), non-ITS computer instruction (0.57) and textbooks (0.35). No difference from individual human tutoring (g -0.11) or small groups (0.05).
numbers: g = 0.42 / 0.57 / 0.35 vs controls; -0.11 vs human tutor; 0.05 vs small group.
limits: Abstract only. Publication-bias test said consistent with positive effect.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as VanLehn: ITS roughly equals a human tutor. Not evidence that the student model itself adds value.

source: Steenbergen-Hu & Cooper (2013) Meta-analysis of ITS on K-12 students' mathematical learning (abstract via ERIC EJ1054449)
finding: 26 reports, 34 samples, 1997-2010. Average effects only g = 0.01 to 0.09 (no harm, perhaps small gain). Larger when the intervention lasted under a school year, and larger for general students than for low achievers.
numbers: g = 0.01 to 0.09 overall; short interventions larger than year-long ones; low achievers gained less.
limits: Abstract only. Mostly ITS versus ordinary classroom, so tutor, curriculum and time all differ.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: an adaptive scaffold may help average cases and widen gaps. Report results by prior-skill level.

source: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity (2026, abstract via ERIC ED682145)
finding: 18 US K-12 studies, 79 effect sizes, 11 ITS: overall g = 0.274. Robust to publication bias. Lower in studies with rural schools and with low differential attrition. Worked-out examples, duration, condition, outcome type and immediate measurement were the top moderators.
numbers: g = 0.274 (SE 0.011), 18 studies, 79 effect sizes, 11 systems.
limits: Abstract only. Smaller than 2013-2016 estimates (0.01-0.09 for math; 0.66 median in Kulik).
agent_relevance: Effects shrink when attrition is controlled and when tests are delayed. Plan delayed checks for any claimed agent gain.

source: Doroudi & Brunskill (2017) The misidentified identifiability problem of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (EDM 2017)
finding: Beck and Chang's 2007 'identifiability problem' is not one: under mild conditions BKT is identifiable (hidden Markov model result). The real problem is semantic degeneracy, where best-fit parameters contradict the idea of mastery. It appears when data come from a different learner model, and changes with sequence length.
numbers: Data from a 10-level mastery model: BKT fit to 500 sequences of 20 steps vs 100 sequences of 200 steps gave different degenerate fits (e.g. P(S)=0.44 with 20 steps, P(G)=0.49 with 200 steps). First fit implies a mastered student answers correctly 56% of the time, truth 90%, so the tutor assigns far fewer problems than needed. Degenerate = guess or slip over 0.5, or no mastery above 0.95 after m=10 correct answers.
quote: Using such a BKT model to determine when a student has had sufficient practice will likely give far fewer problems than they need.
limits: Synthetic data only. Does not show how common degeneracy is in real tutor logs. Parameters found by brute-force grid in 0.01 steps.
agent_relevance: Corrects K16: do not claim 'non-identifiable'. Claim instead that the mastery threshold is only as good as the fitted model; a wrong-form tracker can say 'mastered' too early or too late.

source: Own simulation (this run): BKT fit sensitivity and mastery threshold, script D:/research_scratch/A05.08/tmp/A05.08_bkt_sim2.py
finding: Synthetic well-specified BKT (true L0 0.3, T 0.15, S 0.10, G 0.20), 100 learners x 8 attempts, grid fit. 27 of 19,200 parameter sets lie within 1.92 log-likelihood units of the best. Their mastery calls differ modestly, not wildly.
numbers: Near-best sets: L0 0.20-0.40, T 0.11-0.17, S 0.10-0.14, G 0.22-0.30. Correct answers needed to pass P>=0.95: 3 to 4 (truth 3); at 0.99: 4 to 5 (truth 4). After C,C,I,C,C, 74% of near-best sets say mastered (>=0.95), truth 0.984. After 3 correct, 93% say mastered.
limits: My own synthetic result, not a literature finding. Well-specified model, one seed, coarse grid. Doroudi & Brunskill (d08) show the bigger risk is model misspecification.
agent_relevance: With a correct model the threshold is stable to about one attempt; with one miss in the window the call becomes a coin flip. Use a margin or require two clean runs before the agent stops checking a sub-skill.

source: Schwonke et al. (2009) The worked-example effect: not an artefact of lousy control conditions, Computers in Human Behavior 25, 258-266; plus Salden et al. (2010) EJ880294 and Booth et al. (2013) EJ998490 abstracts
finding: Full text and abstract of Schwonke 2009 could not be reached (ScienceDirect 403; Crossref has no abstract; Semantic Scholar rate-limited). Related abstracts: Salden et al. 2010 (one lab + one classroom experiment): adaptive fading of worked examples beat fixed fading beat plain Cognitive Tutor problem solving. Booth et al. 2013: worked examples with a Cognitive Tutor gave no posttest difference on equation construction but cut learning time on instructional items and hint requests.
numbers: No Schwonke numbers obtained. Salden 2010: adaptive > fixed > problem solving (two experiments). Booth 2013: no paper-and-pencil or delayed difference among 4 groups; control group needed more learning time on examples.
limits: Gap 5 stays OPEN. Also: evidence b28 cites DOI 10.1016/j.learninstruc.2009.02.016, which is a different paper (Meyer, Rasch & Schnotz on animation speed). The correct Schwonke 2009 DOI is 10.1016/j.chb.2008.12.011 (a24).
agent_relevance: Worked examples that fade as the tracker rises are supported at abstract level; the size of the effect is unknown.

source: Worden, Heffernan, Heffernan & Sonkar (2026) FoundationalASSIST, Table 7 and section 6.1.4-6.1.5
finding: The optimism bias differs by model, so it is a property of the model, not of the task. Qwen3-80B-Instruct is nearly balanced. Longer histories do not fix it: AUC stays near 0.5 from 50 to 400 prior interactions. No calibration or verifier was tried.
numbers: Accuracy when student correct / incorrect: GPT-OSS-120B 68.2 / 43.4; Llama-3.3-70B 85.4 / 12.6; Qwen3-80B-Instruct 56.5 / 51.0; Qwen3-80B-Thinking 63.6 / 44.6. Cognitive-modelling accuracy on incorrect answers only 14.5-19.8%. Context 50-400 interactions: no consistent gain.
quote: models default to predicting correct answers because that is overwhelmingly what they have learned to produce
limits: Zero-shot prompts only. Authors' explanation (pretraining on correct reasoning) is untested.
agent_relevance: Model choice changes how well the agent can judge its own failures. Test self-error recall per model before trusting a self-check.

source: Hooshyar et al. (2025) Problems with LLMs for learner modelling, Tables 3-4
finding: Moving the decision threshold is the cheap fix for optimism, and fine-tuning is the stronger one. The zero-shot LLM needed a cut-off of 0.8789 to balance errors, DKT 0.5782, fine-tuned LLM 0.6211. Recall on low performers rose from 20% to 64% after fine-tuning, matching DKT (64%).
numbers: Youden-optimal threshold: DKT 0.5782, zero-shot Llama 3 8B 0.8789, fine-tuned 0.6211. Low-performer recall: DKT 64, zero-shot 20, fine-tuned 64. AUC: 0.83 / 0.69 / 0.77. High-performer recall: 83 / 95 / 78.
limits: One dataset, one 8B model, DKT as the only baseline. Threshold shift changes the error trade-off, not AUC (ranking), so it does not make the model better at telling who will fail.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed: bias is removable by thresholding and fine-tuning, but discrimination stays weak. For the agent: calibrate the self-check cut-off on held-out cases; do not assume a raw 'looks right' signal is balanced.

source: Bhattacharyya et al. (2026) Faster, cheaper, more accurate: KT vs LLMs on Eedi (benchmark section)
finding: A per-question average-correctness baseline (no student model at all) already gets 66.5% accuracy on Eedi, and several LLMs fail to beat it. The best systems add only about 5-6 points on top: LLM KT 72.8%, DKT 71.8%.
numbers: Dataset-bias baseline 66.5% accuracy. Fine-tuned Llama-1B 71.0%, zero-shot Llama-1B 33.5%. F1: LLM KT 0.674, SAKT 0.669, DKT 0.650, GPT-4o-mini 0.579, Qwen2.5-7B 0.533, Gemini-2.5-flash-lite 0.527, Llama-1B LoRA 0.592, Llama-1B zero-shot 0.251.
limits: Item-level baseline is a count of past correctness per question (across students), not a per-student logistic model with recency. Gap 2 still needs a PFA/recency logistic baseline on the same split.
agent_relevance: Most of the available signal is item difficulty (a count). A cheap count-based tracker for the agent's task types likely gets most of the benefit; gap 1 is plausible but still untested directly.

source: Norris, Gal & Bulathwela (2025) Next Token Knowledge Tracing (NTKT), experiment design and Table 1
finding: NTKT's baselines were DKT, AKT, AKT-text and DTransformer. No per-question average, PFA or logistic-with-recency baseline appears. The gain over the best baseline is over 10 AUC points.
numbers: Eedi data 1,905,115 interactions from 39,873 students. NTKT 3B: F1 85.22, accuracy 78.87, AUC 90.32. Even the 1B model beats all baselines. ID-only 77.06 vs DKT 72.37 AUC.
limits: Single group, one dataset. Not cited in the three independent 2025-26 benchmarks I opened (d11-d13). Leakage not discussed. Eedi-style data has about 1.01 skills per question, so the multi-skill leakage that inflated AS2009/AL2005 should be small (d15).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: nobody has put a recency logistic model against an LLM tracer. The large text-based gain is exactly what a text-aware logistic baseline should be tested against.

source: Liu et al. (2022) pyKT, Observation 2 and Table 3 (leakage by dataset)
finding: Leakage from expanded multi-skill sequences inflates AUC by 0.0843-0.1299 on AS2009 and 0.1057-0.2388 on AL2005 (mean +8.38 and +13.09 points) but only 0.0002-0.0017 on BD2006 and 0.0016-0.0067 on NIPS34 (Eedi-derived). Cause: average skills per question 1.1970 and 1.3634 vs 1.0136 and 1.0148.
numbers: Gains from leakage: AS2009 mean 8.38%, AL2005 13.09%, BD2006 and NIPS34 under 1 point.
limits: pyKT does not test LLM tracers. Eedi data in NTKT is a different release from NIPS34, so the comparison is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Leakage cannot explain a gap of 10+ AUC points on Eedi-type data, but it can explain published gains on multi-skill sets. Check which kind of dataset a claimed tracker gain comes from.

source: Li et al. (2025) CIKT, data and split description
finding: CIKT uses an 8:1:1 train/validation/test split and removes learners with under 5 interactions. The text I read has no leakage audit and no external replication. None of the independent benchmarks (d11-d13) include it.
numbers: 8:1:1 split; k=1000 iteration sample; gains level off after about 3 rounds (from K09).
limits: I searched my downloaded benchmark papers by name; I could not run a citation search (Semantic Scholar, arXiv API and OpenAlex rate-limited or exhausted this session).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays OPEN: I found no independent replication of NTKT or CIKT. Treat both as single-group results.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) Exploring knowledge tracing in tutor-student dialogues, human evaluation of GPT-4o labels
finding: Label quality is the weak point. GPT-4o final-turn correctness accuracy was 75.82% on the full CoMTA set (83.33% on the 30-dialogue sample) against 85.56% for expert teachers. Correctness labels are over 90% positive, so chance-corrected agreement is low.
numbers: 3 former maths teachers, 30 dialogues, 166 turn pairs. Correctness score 0.9317/1, overlap 0.8434, agreement statistic 0.1809 (low because over 90% of labels are 1). Knowledge-component score 3.28/4, overlap 0.3494, statistic 0.4383.
limits: No experiment injected noisy labels and measured the AUC drop, so the cost of label noise is not measured. Column names in the garbled table inferred from the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly open: noise exists and is large for the final turn, but its cost to tracing is unmeasured. An agent that labels its own steps right or wrong will have similar skew; track precision on 'wrong' separately.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS (PMC12232635 full text)
finding: Nearly 1,000 students in about 50 classes (grades 9-11), four 90-minute sessions. GPT Base raised practice scores 48% but cut unaided exam scores 17%. GPT Tutor (hints, not answers) raised practice 127% and removed the exam harm, but did not give a positive exam effect. Students in the GPT Base arm did not perceive that they learned less.
numbers: Practice: +48% (Base), +127% (Tutor). Exam: -17% (Base), about 0 (Tutor).
quote: students in the GPT Base arm perform statistically significantly worse than students in the control arm by 17%
limits: Maths only; exam taken inside the same programme, not weeks later. Guardrails removed harm; they did not produce gain.
agent_relevance: Correction to K11: the guardrail removed harm but did not raise unaided performance. Learners (and agents) misjudge their own learning when given answers.

source: Lehmann, Cornelius & Sting (2025) AI meets the classroom: when do LLMs harm learning?
finding: Python programming, not maths. Two preregistered lab experiments found no overall effect of LLM access. How the LLM was used mattered: asking for solutions raised topic coverage but lowered understanding; asking for explanations raised understanding. A field study (two graduate courses, outage-based identification) found a long-term decline. LLMs widened the gap between low and high prior knowledge.
numbers: Study 1 field: 113 students, 6,594 observations; same-question grade +0.18 per unit of ChatGPT similarity, cumulative -0.02. Study 2: N=107, treated mean 4.45 messages, post-test not significant (p=0.206). Study 3: N=69, learning phase +4 questions (p=0.003), post-test +2 (p=0.092), post-minus-pre p=0.312.
limits: Small lab samples, 45-minute learning phase, mostly novices. Exploratory usage analysis is not randomised. Field delay is within a course.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed: the 'own step before help' effect does carry to coding, and the harm is from substitution use, not from LLM access itself.

source: Beyond the 'Wow' factor: ChatTutor for generative sense-making (2025, abstract via ERIC EJ1474143)
finding: Two experiments with delayed follow-up (psychology course N=175, preregistered; high school N=234). A pedagogically designed chatbot beat generic ChatGPT on conceptual knowledge immediately in both studies and at follow-up in Study 2. Versus teaching as usual or re-study, the edge was only partly significant.
numbers: N=175 and N=234; ChatTutor > ChatGPT in conceptual knowledge (immediate: both; follow-up: Study 2 only). Vs control: significant only at follow-up in Study 1, and immediate in Study 2.
limits: Abstract only. Follow-up length not stated. Conceptual knowledge, not skill.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: guardrail-style design helps over a plain assistant on non-math content, with mixed durability against ordinary teaching.

source: Parent-led vs AI-guided dialogic reading, RCT with young EFL children (2025, abstract via ERIC EJ1479944)
finding: 67 children aged 5-8. A scaffolded LLM reading partner beat parent-led reading on comprehension, with comparable vocabulary and retelling gains, both immediately and at delayed tests.
numbers: N=67; AI-led > parent-led on reading comprehension, immediate and delayed.
limits: Abstract only. Small N, one language setting, scaffolding built in (questions), so it is not an unguarded assistant.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a delayed, non-math positive for a scaffolded LLM. Not a test of 'own step first'.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your brain on ChatGPT (essay writing, MIT)
finding: 54 adults wrote essays in three groups (LLM, search engine, brain-only), 18 per group; 18 returned for session 4 with groups switched. LLM users had weaker neural coupling, lower reported ownership and weaker ability to quote their own essay.
numbers: N=54 over sessions 1-3, 18 in session 4. No delayed knowledge test with scores in my read.
limits: Preprint, small N, EEG and interviews; not a learning-outcome test. Treat as a hypothesis generator only.
agent_relevance: Weak support for gap 8 outside maths: offloading the first step may reduce what is retained. Not decisive.

source: Two 2025-26 meta-analyses of ChatGPT on achievement (ERIC EJ1501298; EJ1478249)
finding: Pooled effects of ChatGPT use on achievement are moderate and positive: g = 0.573 (22 publications) and g = 0.577 (37 studies, 95% CI 0.395-0.759). No significant differences by education level in either.
numbers: g = 0.573 (22 publications, Nov 2022-Dec 2024); g = 0.577 (37 effect sizes).
limits: Abstracts only. Mostly short studies with immediate tests, many without guardrails; this conflicts with Bastani and Lehmann unless the outcome is measured unaided and later.
agent_relevance: Large positive averages come from assisted or immediate tests. Keep unaided, delayed scoring in any agent test.
